answers.text: For example: always answer in exactly three lines, same order every time — delivery date, then item and quantity, then any change from the order. Nothing else gets added in.

I would make sure the memo always lists date, amount, category and submitter in the same order every week, so it is easy to read. And I would keep the wording friendly so people don't mind reading it.
My first thought is the price total, 100 times 48.50 — I would want someone to look at that again before this goes out.
62 up from 54 is about 15%, that checks out. The late-delivery number and the stock split both look fine to me on a quick read.
I would sign off on the second one, since it gives the actual sales and returns figures — 612,000 and 25,100 — not just the 4.1%. The first one leaves out where that number comes from.
I would go with the second reply, it has the order and credit numbers in it. The first is warmer in tone but you cannot check anything in it.
1. No. 2. Yes. 3. No. 4. No, safer not to. 5. No.
I would take out the pricing details before pasting anything in, and go carefully with the confidentiality part since it names both sides directly.
Before the report goes to the manager, I would check the totals myself against warehouse system.
Step one is where mistakes start if the reading is wrong, but step four worries me more, since it sends the confirmation on its own — someone should look at it first.
